newsitem.title: MEXICO: Voting violence in Mexico state sparks fears.
newsitem.headline: Voting violence in Mexico state sparks fears.

text.p: Mobs of angry Mexican Indians demolished dozens of polling stations and blocked roads in the troubled southern state of Chiapas during national elections on Sunday, sparking fears the vote there may have to be annulled.

The Indians, supporters of the state's Mayan Zapatista rebels and some of them wearing masks, destroyed polling stations in the remote central highlands of the impoverished state, preventing electors from voting in the key mid-term poll.

Officials in Chiapas denied earlier reports that a bridge had been blown up in the town of Ocosingo and declined comment on other incidents, but witnesses said voting papers had been burned and polling booths destroyed in a number of areas.
Election monitors said they feared the vote in the troubled state would have to be declared invalid.

"There may have to be an annulment of the election in Chiapas because of the events there," said Emilio Alvarez Icaza, a spokesman for private electoral watchdog Alianza Civica. "They may have to rerun the vote."
The executive secretary of Mexico's national electoral institute (IFE) said 59 polling booths had not been installed in three of Chiapas' 12 voting districts.

But estimates based on findings by Alianza Civica showed 89 polling booths were not functioning in three districts inhabited by Zapatista sympathisers. At least 25 were destroyed, or burned to the ground and their ballots stolen.

Witnesses said dozens of Indians stormed polling stations in the villages of San Andres Larrainzar and Tzuben, both about 400 miles (660 km) southeast of Mexico City, tearing down voting booths and setting fire to ballots.
"Get out, get out," they shouted to local election officials in San Andres, who scrambled from the city square.
Polling centres were also destroyed in the nearby colonial city of San Cristobal de las Casas, the city of Ocosingo, and the towns of Tenejapa and Altamirano, witnesses said.

The protests followed a call by Zapatista rebel leader Subcommander Marcos earlier in the week for an election boycott to protest a lack of progress in stalled peace talks between the government and the Maya Indian guerrillas.
Mexicans were voting on Sunday for most of a new Congress, six state governors and a first-ever Mexico City mayor.
The Zapatistas launched an uprising for Indian rights and democracy on New Year's Day 1994, but have since been mired in on-and-off peace talks with the government.

After Marcos called the boycott, federal election officials decided not to install 23 polling stations in so-called Zapatista territory, a swathe of land in the state controlled by rebels and home to about 40,000 Indians.
Zapatista supporters had vowed late on Saturday to block voting booths in certain parts of the state, even outside Zapatista-controlled territory.
The Zapatistas, disillusioned with local authorities, do not recognise most of Chiapas's elected officials and have set up parallel governments, with "rebel" mayors and city councillors.
